title: The Chronicles of Riddick
full_review:
In 2000, before he achieved action-star status, Vin Diesel made a small, rather intriguing sci-fi film, "Pitch Black," which went white-hot once it was released on DVD. "The Chronicles of Riddick" (Universal) is its sequel, a big-budget summer movie with lots of bluster and special effects. It's not the kind of sequel where you need to have seen the first to comprehend the second; it's just that the better choice is to see the first and maybe skip the second -- even though a third and a fourth will materialize if "Chronicles" turns blockbuster.

Diesel is the antihero Riddick of the title, an escaped convict pursued by bounty hunters five years later who lands on the planet Helion. The besieged humans there, called Elementals, are in danger of extinction by steely Necromonger warriors led by their despotic Lord Marshal (Colm Feore). Marshal is set on conquering them and giving them a choice: Die or become one of his robotic Necromongers.

Urging Riddick to stand up to Marshal is Elemental ambassador Aereon (the sagelike Judi Dench) who appears and vanishes at will, reminding Riddick that because of his Furion ancestry only he is capable of killing the seemingly all-powerful Marshal. Riddick, however, is captured and thrust into a subterranean prison where he reunites with now grown-up rebel Kyra (Alexa Davalos) and saves her from snarling monsters before they escape.

Meanwhile, the ambitious wife (Thandie Newton) of Marshal's loyal soldier Vaako (Karl Urban) is conspiring to advance her husband no matter the cost. This couple and Kyra will figure significantly in the inevitable final face-off between Marshal and Riddick.

For all its density of plot and frequent shootouts, writer-director David Twohy's script lags, with the necessary sense of urgency distinctly lacking. He seems more concerned with being a director of action sequences and overseeing massive special effects. The characters, unfortunately, are left underdeveloped and end up being dull. The sexual tension that is supposed to be building between Kyra and Riddick essentially fizzles, so the highly emotional ending is not very convincing.

The production design, however, is outstanding -- and on a grand scale. The narrative may be murky but one can be distracted in the good sense by the many elaborate sets in this intergalactic world of icy nights and scorching sunrises. Yet such excellent art direction ends up as little more than an ineffective backdrop when front and center features so much empty male posturing. In fact, Diesel seems to grunt his way through the story, as if diction and dialogue were outside his ken. The violence is not very disturbing, shot as it is in a blurry, mostly stylized fashion with little gore. The target young male audience may find the movie exciting, but those not awed by Diesel will find it sputters.

Because of recurring stylized violence, minimal profanity and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
